blocks.text: “Thanks, and thanks, and thanks again for your sweet letter. It was so nice to be able to tell you and to have your sympathy.

“My dear, people say ‘it never rains but it pours’. When something happens, a lot of it happens at once. How true the old sayings are. I will be twenty in September. Until today, no man had ever asked me to marry him—not a real proposal. And today I have had three. Just imagine! THREE proposals in one day! Isn’t it awful! I feel sorry, really and truly sorry, for two of the poor men. Oh, Mina, I am so happy that I don’t know what to do with myself. And three proposals! But please, don’t tell any of the other girls. If you do, they will get all sorts of wild ideas. They will feel hurt and insulted if they don’t get at least six on their very first day at home. Some girls are so vain! You and I, Mina dear, are engaged. Soon we will settle down quietly and seriously as old married women. So we can look down on vanity. Well, I must tell you about the three. But you must keep it a secret from everyone, dear—except, of course, Jonathan. You will tell him. If I were in your place, I would certainly tell Arthur. A woman should tell her husband everything—don’t you think so, dear? And I must be fair. Men like women to be just as fair as they are—certainly their wives. And I am afraid that women are not always as fair as they should be. Well, my dear, number One came just before lunch. I told you about him before. He is Dr. John Seward, the lunatic-asylum man—the man from the hospital for mad people. He has a strong jaw and a good forehead. On the outside he seemed very calm, but he was nervous all the same. He had clearly practised all sorts of little things beforehand, and he remembered them. But he nearly sat down on his silk hat. Men don’t usually do that when they are calm. Then he wanted to look relaxed, so he kept playing with a lancet—a small, sharp knife that doctors use. The way he played with it nearly made me scream. He spoke to me very honestly and directly, Mina. He told me how much he loved me, even though he had known me for such a short time. He told me what his life would be like with me there to help him and cheer him. He was going to tell me how unhappy he would be if I did not care for him. But when he saw me cry, he said he was a brute. He said he would not add to the trouble I was already in. Then he stopped and asked if I could love him in time. I shook my head, and his hands trembled. Then, a little unsure, he asked me if I already cared for someone else. He asked it very kindly. He said he did not want to force my secret out of me. He only wanted to know, because if a woman’s heart was free, a man might have hope. And then, Mina, I felt it was a kind of duty to tell him that there was someone. I only told him that much. Then he stood up. He looked very strong and very serious. He took both my hands in his and said he hoped I would be happy. He said that if I ever needed a friend, I must think of him as one of my best. Oh, Mina dear, I can’t stop crying. Please forgive me for all the ink stains on this letter. Getting a proposal is all very nice, and all that sort of thing. But it isn’t a happy thing at all when you have to watch a poor man go away. You know he loves you honestly, and he leaves looking completely broken-hearted. And you know that you are going right out of his life, whatever he may say at the moment. My dear, I must stop here for now. I feel so miserable, even though I am so happy.

“Arthur has just left. I feel more cheerful than when I stopped writing, so I can go on telling you about the day. Well, my dear, number Two came after lunch. He is such a nice man, an American from Texas. He looks so young and so fresh. It seems almost impossible that he has been to so many places and had such adventures. I feel for poor Desdemona, who had such a dangerous stream of words poured into her ear, even by a black man. I suppose we women are such cowards. We think a man will save us from our fears, and so we marry him. Now I know what I would do if I were a man and wanted to make a girl love me. No, I don’t. Mr. Morris was always telling us his stories, and Arthur never told any, and yet—— My dear, I am getting ahead of myself. Mr. Quincey P. Morris found me alone. It seems that a man always does find a girl alone. No, he doesn’t. Arthur tried twice to make a chance, and I helped him all I could. I am not ashamed to say it now. First I must tell you something. Mr. Morris doesn’t always speak slang. In fact, he never uses it with strangers or in front of them, because he is really well educated and has beautiful manners. But he found out that I enjoyed hearing him talk American slang. So whenever I was there, and there was no one to be shocked, he said such funny things. I am afraid, my dear, that he has to invent it all, because it fits so exactly with everything else he says. But slang is like that. I don’t know if I will ever speak slang myself. I don’t know if Arthur likes it, because I have never heard him use any yet. Well, Mr. Morris sat down beside me. He looked as happy and cheerful as he could, but I could still see that he was very nervous. He took my hand in his and said very sweetly:—
